title: C# Questions & Answers - Collection Classes
sourceFile: Collection Classes - C# Questions & Answers - Sanfoundry.html
description: This section of our 1000+ C# MCQs focuses on collection in classes in C# Programming Language.

questions.question: Which among the following is not an ordered sequential collection (FIFO/LIFO) in System.Collections?
questions.explanation: Queue is FIFO and Stack is LIFO. BitArray is a compact array of bits addressed by index, not a sequential FIFO/LIFO collection. (BitArray is still index-ordered; it is simply not a queue or stack.)

questions.question: Which among the following is not an interface declared in the System.Collections namespace?
questions.explanation: System.Collections defines IEnumerable, IEnumerator, IComparer, IComparer, IDictionary, IDictionaryEnumerator, and others. There is no IDictionaryComparer. (The original option Icomparer is the same as IComparer, just misspelled.)

questions.question: Which among the following is the correct way to find out the number of elements currently present in an ArrayList called arr?
questions.explanation: ArrayList.Count is the number of elements stored. Capacity is the allocated size, which may be larger than Count.

questions.question: Which statement is correct in the following C#.NET code snippet?

options.text: Unsimilar elements like "Csharp", 7.3, 8 cannot be stored in the same stack collection
Boolean values can never be stored in Stack collection

questions.explanation: Non-generic Stack stores object, so values of different types are boxed and pushed. The snippet compiles and runs. (Prefer Stack<T> in new code.)

questions.question: Which is the correct statement about an ArrayList collection that implements the IEnumerable interface?

options.text: To access members of ArrayList from the inner class, it is necessary to pass ArrayList class reference to it
The inner class of ArrayList can access ArrayList class members
The ArrayList class consist of inner class that implements the IEnumerator interface

questions.explanation: ArrayList implements IEnumerable. GetEnumerator returns an enumerator object (historically a nested type) that implements IEnumerator and can see the list's items. foreach uses that enumerator.

questions.question: Which among the following is the correct way to access all the elements of the Stack collection created using the C#.NET code snippet given below?
questions.explanation: GetEnumerator() returns IEnumerator, which has MoveNext and Current. IEnumerable is the collection side (GetEnumerator), not the enumerator. There is no GetEnumerable().

questions.question: The correct code to access all the elements of the queue collection created using the following C#.NET code snippets?
questions.explanation: Same pattern as Stack: IEnumerator from GetEnumerator(), then MoveNext/Current. Option b uses the wrong interface type; option c is invalid.

questions.question: Which statements among the following are correct about the Collection Classes available in Framework Class Library?

options.text: Elements of a collection cannot be transmitted over a network
Elements stored in a collection can be modified only if all the elements are of similar types
Elements stored in a Collection can be retrieved but cannot be modified
Collection classes make use of efficient algorithms to manage the collection, hence improving the performance of the program

questions.explanation: a–c are false: collections can be serialized, can hold mixed object items (non-generic), and items can be updated. Collection types exist to store and manage groups of objects efficiently.

questions.question: Among the given collections which are index-based?
questions.explanation: ArrayList and List<T> expose an integer indexer. Non-generic Stack and Queue do not provide an indexer; you use Push/Pop or Enqueue/Dequeue (and Peek).

questions.question: Which among the given statements are correct about the Stack collection?

options.text: It can be used for evaluation of expressions
It is used to maintain a LIFO list
Top most element of the Stack collection can be accessed using the Peek()

questions.explanation: A stack is LIFO (last in, first out), also described as FILO. Peek() returns the top without removing it. Stacks are used in expression evaluation and parsing. (The original option said FILO, which is the same idea as LIFO.)

questions.question: A Hashtable t maps state names (keys) to capital cities (values). Which call checks whether the capital "New Delhi" is present?
questions.explanation: Capitals are stored as values, so use ContainsValue. ContainsKey looks up a state name. Hashtable has no HasValue or HasKey. (New Delhi is a capital, not a state; the original item treated it as a key.)

questions.question: In which of the following collections is the I/O based on a key?
questions.explanation: SortedList stores key/value pairs and is accessed by key (and also by index). BitArray is index-based; Queue and Stack are sequential.

questions.question: The wrong statements about a Hashtable collection are?

options.text: It implements a IDictionaryEnumerator interface in its inner class

questions.explanation: Hashtable is a keyed, unordered dictionary. Enumeration order is not sorted. It is not index-based. GetEnumerator returns IDictionaryEnumerator.
